Fee management

One parent pays once, for every child

A father with three children in your school hands the clerk one bundle of cash. Most software makes the clerk do that three times, once per child, and prints three receipts. This does it once, and the receipt lists all three children with what each of them owed.

What a monthly fee run actually involves

Not "generate challans". These are the parts that take a clerk's morning, and the parts a spreadsheet gets wrong.

Fee heads and per class structures

Tuition, admission, exam, transport, whatever your school charges, each as its own head. Amounts are set per class, so class 9 and Play Group are not forced onto the same figure, and a change to next month's amounts does not rewrite last month's bills.

Arrears that carry themselves forward

An unpaid month is not silently dropped when the next challan is issued. It is carried, it appears on the new challan as arrears, and the total a parent owes is one number rather than a stack of slips the office has to add up by hand.

Partial payments, and what is left

A parent pays Rs 2,000 of a Rs 5,800 bill. The receipt says so, the balance says so, and the next reminder is for the remainder rather than for the whole bill again. Nobody has to remember what was paid on the counter last Tuesday.

Discounts that somebody approved

A discount is not a number a clerk can type into a total. It is recorded against the pupil with a reason and the name of whoever allowed it, so a concession granted quietly is a concession you can find. Fines work the same way.

Fee control

Know what should have been collected

Most school software tells you what was collected. That number is only useful if you already trust it. The harder and more valuable question is what the roll says should have arrived, and where the difference went.

Nothing here is an accusation. Most of the gap in most schools is a mistake in the record, corrected by a reversal that leaves both entries in place with a reason and a name attached.

  • Expected against collected: class by class, from the real roll.
  • Ghost student check: anyone being billed who never appears in a register.
  • Discounts need approval. A clerk proposes, the principal approves, both are recorded.
  • Cash drawer settlement: each collector counts their own drawer, and a difference needs a written reason.
  • Full audit trail: every change to money, marks and attendance, with who and when.

Receipt numbers that cannot skip

Every receipt is issued in an unbroken sequence, and nothing is ever deleted. That single rule is what makes the rest of it checkable.

If a receipt could be deleted, a missing number would mean nothing: it could be a cancelled sale, a printer jam or cash that never reached the drawer, and there would be no way to tell which. Because a mistake is corrected by a reversal rather than a deletion, a gap in the sequence is always a question with an answer, and the answer is in the record with a name against it.
